title: Kafka: why it exists (the World Cup example)
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: The problem Kafka solves, step by step: one queue, too many events, ordering, partitions, consumer groups and topics.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: What is Kafka, in one sentence?

options.text: An open-source, distributed event streaming platform usable as a message queue or a stream.
options.why: Right: both uses on the same log.

options.text: A relational database with SQL joins and foreign keys.
options.why: Kafka is not a database.

options.text: A caching layer that holds data only in memory.
options.why: It stores messages durably on disk.

options.text: A load balancer that spreads HTTP requests in a typical production setup.
options.why: It moves messages, not HTTP traffic.

questions.explanation: With proper replication and acknowledgements, messages are very hard to lose.

questions.prompt: A queue hosted on one server receives events from 1,000 simultaneous games. What goes wrong?

options.text: The single queue server cannot keep up, and the consumer is overwhelmed like a firehose.
options.why: Right: a single server is the bottleneck.

options.text: Events are silently turned into images for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Not a real behaviour; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The events become ordered across all games.
options.why: Order is the hard part, not a guaranteed result.

options.text: Nothing; one server scales without limit under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Every server has limits.

questions.explanation: Adding servers is easy; keeping events in order while you do it is hard.

questions.prompt: Why does spreading events randomly across servers break the stats site?

options.text: One match's events end up on different servers and are read in a mixed-up order.
options.why: Right: goals can appear before kick-off.

options.text: Random spreading makes every event arrive twice in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Duplicates are a different issue.

options.text: Random spreading deletes older events.
options.why: Nothing is deleted; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Servers refuse events they did not choose under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Not a real rule; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: We need a smarter rule for where each event goes.

questions.prompt: What is the fix for order within a game?

options.text: Send all events of one game to the same queue, which Kafka calls a partition.
options.why: Right: same game, same queue, same order.

options.text: Sort every event by timestamp at the website.
options.why: That does not fix the distributed ordering problem at the source.

options.text: Make one giant queue for all games on a single server in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That brings back the bottleneck.

options.text: Read events from all servers at the same time and hope for the best as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Order would still be mixed.

questions.explanation: Order is only guaranteed inside one partition, so things that must stay in order share a key.

questions.prompt: What is the rule of a consumer group?

options.text: Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group.
options.why: Right: events are not split across consumers.

options.text: Each consumer reads every partition at the same time in a typical production setup.
options.why: That would duplicate work.

options.text: Each partition is read by all consumers, who then vote without any extra configuration.
options.why: There is no voting; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: A group can have only one consumer.
options.why: Many consumers share the work.

questions.explanation: Partitions split the data; a consumer group splits the work on those partitions.

questions.prompt: True or false: Kafka's default at-least-once delivery means a message could be re-processed after a failure, but it is never split across consumers in the group.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: duplicates are possible on failure.

options.text: False
options.why: Re-processing after failure is possible, so make processing safe.

questions.explanation: Under normal operation each event reaches a single consumer; failures can cause a repeat.

questions.prompt: The soccer website must not see basketball events. What does Kafka provide?

options.text: Topics: every event is published to a topic and consumers subscribe only to the topics they need.
options.why: Right: topics organise the data.

options.text: A separate Kafka cluster for each sport only as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Topics do this inside one cluster.

options.text: A filter that every consumer must write by hand on the key for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Topics are the built-in mechanism.

options.text: A single partition shared by all sports.
options.why: That would mix them; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Topics organise your data; partitions scale your data.
